outcome: Nothing since 26 January 2024 has changed the status of Agrawal's conjecture: no proof, no disproof and no verified counterexample has appeared. The only in-window items touching AKS (an April 2025 bounded-arithmetic paper and a January 2026 randomised-AKS preprint, withdrawn 24 September 2026) do not concern this congruence.
problem_asks: For all coprime positive integers n and r: if (X - 1)^n ≡ X^n - 1 (mod n, X^r - 1), then n is prime or n^2 ≡ 1 (mod r). Parts: (1) the hypothesis, a congruence of polynomials over Z/nZ taken modulo X^r - 1, i.e. modulo the ideal generated by n and X^r - 1; (2) the conclusion, a disjunction, n is prime or n^2 ≡ 1 (mod r), read inclusively; (3) the quantifier, universal over all coprime pairs (n, r). A single pair with n composite, the congruence holding, and n^2 not ≡ 1 (mod r) falsifies it. Verifying finitely many pairs settles nothing about the universal claim. The statement asks for no bound, no algorithm and no size for r. Wording variant: Wikipedia and the 2003 AIM note take n and r merely coprime; the Grokipedia summary says the Popovych-style presentation takes r prime and not dividing n, and that some presentations allow any coprime r.

events.what_happened: AIM problem note 'Remarks on Agrawal's Conjecture', from the AIM workshop 'Future directions in algorithmic number theory' (held March 2003, organised by Lenstra, Pomerance and Pila). It states the conjecture and records a proposition credited to Lenstra: for n = p_1...p_k a product of distinct primes with k ≡ 1 (mod 4), p_i ≡ 3 (mod 80), (p_i - 1) | (n - 1) and (p_i + 1) | (n + 1), the congruence (X - 1)^n ≡ X^n - 1 (mod n, X^5 - 1) holds while n^2 ≢ 1 (mod 5). It notes the result also holds for k ≡ 3 (mod 4). It gives a Lenstra–Pomerance heuristic that such n are abundant (counterexamples up to x expected to be ≫ x^(1-ε)) and says the contents 'suggest strongly that this conjecture is false'. No prime set or n is exhibited.
events.delivers: Conditionally: any n = p_1...p_k meeting the stated prime conditions (with k ≡ 1 mod 4) is a composite counterexample to the conjecture with r = 5. Unconditionally, no counterexample: no such prime set is exhibited. The abundance claim is a heuristic, not a proof.
events.remains: Whether any prime set with the stated conditions exists (the note's heuristic says yes; unproven). The conjecture for all coprime (n, r), including whether counterexamples exist at all. The r = 5 family is one route only.

checked_by.qualification: Number theorist who published a generalisation of this proposition in 2009 (see popovych-2009-eprint)
checked_by.what_they_did: Proved the Lenstra proposition holds in a more general case (per the ePrint abstract)

events.directly_checkable: For any candidate n and r = 5, the congruence and n^2 mod 5 are a finite computation. The note gives no candidate, so nothing has been checked in practice.
events.doubts: The family's hypotheses concern primes the note does not exhibit; existence rests on a heuristic. The note's r = 5 proof is a sketch that reduces the congruence to checks in F_p[ζ5] for each prime p. I did not verify the sketch line by line. The 2019 OEIS comment (oeis-a329223-2019) records that no explicit term meeting the Carmichael/Lucas-Carmichael route is known.
events.direction: Cuts against the conjecture, conditionally: it gives a family that would be counterexamples for r = 5 if the primes exist, and the authors say the conjecture is strongly suspected false. It produces no counterexample.
events.object: A family of composites n = p_1...p_k (k ≡ 1 mod 4; each p_i ≡ 3 mod 80; (p_i - 1) | (n - 1); (p_i + 1) | (n + 1)). For each such n the note shows (X - 1)^n ≡ X^n - 1 (mod n, X^5 - 1) and n^2 ≢ 1 (mod 5). Non-constructive: the note exhibits no member, and existence is heuristic.

events.what_happened: Roman B. Popovych, 'A note on Agrawal conjecture', IACR Cryptology ePrint Archive 2009/008, received 5 January 2009. Per the abstract it: proves that the Lenstra proposition (many counterexamples exist) holds in a more general case; obtains a strictly ascending chain of subgroups of (Z_p[X]/(C_r(X)))*; and states a modified conjecture that {X-1, X+2} generates a sufficiently large subgroup of that group. Wikipedia dates it 2008. I read only the abstract page; the PDF was not readable.
events.delivers: Extends the Lenstra proposition's conditional counterexample family to a more general setting, per the abstract. The full text, which would give the exact generality, was not readable to me. It does not produce a counterexample to the original conjecture. The modified conjecture it states is a different claim; Wikipedia describes it as adding a second congruence (X+2)^n ≡ X^n + 2 (mod n, X^r - 1).
events.remains: The original conjecture entirely. The modified conjecture is stated, not proved. Whether the generalised proposition yields any explicit counterexample.
events.doubts: IACR ePrint is unrefereed. I read only the abstract, so the scope of the claimed generalisation is unknown to me. Wikipedia's 2008 date and the ePrint's received date of 2009-01-05 differ. I found no third-party engagement with this note's argument beyond citations.
events.direction: Strengthens, indirectly, the conditional case against the original conjecture by extending the family. The modified conjecture it proposes is a separate open question.

events.what_happened: Roman B. Popovych, 'Lower bounds on the orders of subgroups connected with Agrawal conjecture', Carpathian Mathematical Publications 5(2) (2013), 310–314, DOI 10.15330/cmp.5.2.310-314, published online 30 December 2013 (per a search snippet). It gives explicit lower bounds on multiplicative orders of subgroups of a finite field connected with the primality-proving algorithm. Its introduction, as seen in a snippet, says a heuristic suggests the conjecture is false and that some variant may still be true. The journal page and PDF both returned a certificate error to my fetch.
events.revisions: No earlier preprint found. The known date is the journal's online publication, 2013-12-30, so only the year is given.
events.delivers: Lower bounds on subgroup orders in the chain that the modified conjecture concerns. These are tools, not a verdict on the original conjecture or on the modified one.

checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for this paper
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper (per the journal listing in a search snippet)

events.doubts: I did not read the full text, only the abstract and introduction in a search snippet.
events.direction: Neutral on the conjecture. It gives technical lower bounds for subgroups in the modified conjecture's chain and decides neither version.

events.what_happened: Primaboinca, a BOINC volunteer-computing project, searched 10^10 < n < 10^17 for counterexamples to Agrawal's conjecture and to Popovych's modified conjecture. It ran about ten years and was closed on 31 May 2020. The project site states 'no counterexamples for the investigated conjectures were found', and gives final statistics of 27,596,610 workunits, 26,023 hosts and 6,237 users. Wikipedia gives the run as 2010 to 2020. I did not confirm the r values searched.
events.delivers: A finite negative search: no counterexample with n in (10^10, 10^17) for the r values searched, which I could not confirm. A finite check of a universal claim moves nothing the problem asks about and says nothing about all n and r.
events.remains: All of it, including n above 10^17 and r outside the searched set.
events.directly_checkable: The test is re-runnable for any given n and r by computing the congruence and n^2 mod r. I did not inspect the project's code or result logs.
events.doubts: The heuristic predicts counterexamples of low density (count ≫ x^(1-ε) up to x). A null search over this range therefore tests the heuristic only weakly. The operator name 'Steffen Reith' comes from a search snippet and is not on the page I read.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture in the searched range; no counterexample.
people: Steffen Reith (operator; from a search snippet, not confirmed on the site)

events.what_happened: Wikipedia attributes to Kayal and Saxena, in a 2002 technical report, a computational check finding no counterexample for r < 100 and n < 10^10. Grokipedia gives n ≤ 10^11 for the same r range. I could not open the report. The aug02.pdf fetch returned an unreadable binary, and I found no HTML copy. This claim is unverified.
events.delivers: If accurate, finite checks for r < 100 and n < 10^10 (or 10^11 per Grokipedia). These are instance checks of a universal claim.
events.doubts: Primary source unread. The two secondary sources disagree on the bound (10^10 against 10^11).
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture in the stated range.

events.what_happened: Wikipedia cites a December 2014 talk by Saxena reporting a check for r = 5 and n < 10^11. I found no talk, slides or write-up in two searches. The claim is unverified.
events.delivers: If accurate, a finite check for r = 5 and n < 10^11. An instance check only.
events.doubts: The talk could not be located, so its existence and content are unconfirmed.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture in the stated range.

events.what_happened: Tomáš Váňa, 'Agrawal's Conjecture and Carmichael Numbers', student conference paper, Comenius University Bratislava, 2009 (advisor Martin Mačaj). From search snippets only, its contents are: AKS and Carmichael numbers; Agrawal's conjecture, with special cases and an algorithm for computing parameters that test the conjecture faster; experimental data; and an alternative proof of a Lenstra–Pomerance theorem that suggests a way to find a counterexample. The PDF came back as an unreadable binary from both hosts I tried, so I have not opened it.
events.delivers: Not established from what I could read. Per the snippet, it offers special-case analysis and an alternative proof of the Lenstra–Pomerance theorem, which is the conditional family. Whether it reports any counterexample or verification result is unknown to me.
events.remains: All of the conjecture, as far as I can tell.
events.doubts: Student work whose content I have not read. My description rests on search-result snippets alone. I found no evaluation of it.
events.direction: Not established. The snippet suggests it supports the Lenstra–Pomerance route, but I did not read it.

events.what_happened: Agrawal, Kayal and Saxena, 'PRIMES is in P', dated 6 August 2002 (Annals of Mathematics 160 (2004), 781–793). It gives a deterministic polynomial-time primality test. Per Grokipedia, a secondary source, its Future Work section discusses Agrawal's conjecture. I could not open the PDF, so I have not verified that mention.
events.revisions: Journal version Annals of Mathematics 2004, per Wikipedia.
events.delivers: Primality testing through the congruence (X + a)^n ≡ X^n + a (mod n, X^r - 1) for suitable r. This is a different statement from Agrawal's congruence and does not decide it.
events.remains: All of Agrawal's conjecture. The conjecture is the proposed route to a faster variant, which would run in Õ((log n)^3) if true, per Wikipedia.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper, Annals 160(2), 2004, per the Wikipedia citation

events.direction: Not about the conjecture. Its bearing is only the future-work mention, which I did not verify.

events.what_happened: Lenstra and Pomerance, 'Primality testing with Gaussian periods'. A lecture at FSTTCS 2002 (LNCS 2556, Springer) and a preliminary version dated 20 July 2005 (per Wikipedia). The journal version is J. Eur. Math. Soc. 21 (2019), 1229–1269, published 9 January 2019 (per the EMS page, which I opened). It gives a deterministic AKS-type primality test using Gaussian periods, with an improved exponent. Wikipedia also lists a 'Lenstra and Pomerance 2003' variant, so the dates conflict.
events.revisions: Preliminary version 20 July 2005; journal version 9 January 2019 (per Wikipedia and the EMS page).
events.delivers: A deterministic AKS-type primality test with a better exponent. It is a variant of AKS, not the Agrawal congruence. The EMS page does not mention Agrawal's conjecture.

checked_by.who: Journal of the European Mathematical Society
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the variant in 2019. This is not a check of the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Chan Hing Lun Joseph, 'Primality Testing is Polynomial-time: A Mechanised Verification of the AKS Algorithm', PhD thesis, Australian National University, issued 2019. The abstract says it formalises AKS correctness and complexity in the HOL4 prover, with a finite-field and algebra library. It does not mention Agrawal's conjecture or the condition n^2 ≡ 1 (mod r). I opened the repository record and abstract only.
events.delivers: A machine-checked HOL4 formalisation of the AKS algorithm. It is not about Agrawal's conjecture.
events.doubts: The abstract says the work 'aim[s] at' correctness and complexity. I could not confirm from the abstract that the formalisation has no gaps.

events.what_happened: Segawa and Tamaki, IPSJ technical report (2004). Per a search snippet giving the English abstract, for every composite n ≤ 10^11 and every Carmichael number n ≤ 10^16 they find an AKS witness (r, 1) with r ≤ 0.49 log n, and (r, a) with r ≤ 0.37 log n. The report is in Japanese, and I did not open it.
events.delivers: AKS witness data for composites up to 10^11. It concerns AKS witnesses, not the Agrawal congruence or the n^2 ≡ 1 (mod r) condition.
events.doubts: Read from a search snippet only. The full report is in Japanese.

events.what_happened: OEIS A329223, 'Poulet numbers (Fermat pseudoprimes to base 2) that are congruent to 3 or 27 mod 80 with all prime factors ≡ 3 mod 80', by Daniel Suteu, 8 November 2019. A comment says: 'If a term of this sequence is also a Carmichael number and a Lucas-Carmichael number, then it would be a counterexample to Agrawal's conjecture', attributed to Lenstra and Pomerance. Another comment says the only Carmichael term below 2^64 in the sequence, 330468624532072027, is not Lucas-Carmichael. A search snippet also says no term with five prime factors is known to the author.
events.delivers: A sufficient condition for a counterexample within a candidate family: a term that is both Carmichael and Lucas-Carmichael. No such term is listed. This establishes nothing.
events.directly_checkable: Membership in the sequence and the Carmichael and Lucas-Carmichael tests are finite checks for any given term.
events.direction: Neutral. It records a candidate-search route and a dead end.

events.what_happened: Raheleh Jalali and Ondřej Ježil, 'Feasibility of Primality in Bounded Arithmetic', arXiv:2504.17041. It proves the correctness of AKS inside a bounded arithmetic theory, from two algebraic axioms, one a generalised Fermat's little theorem and one a root axiom over a definable finite field. The abstract does not mention Agrawal's conjecture. I opened the abstract page only.
events.revisions: v1 23 April 2025; v2 27 January 2026 (per the arXiv page).
events.delivers: A proof-complexity result: AKS correctness is provable in a bounded arithmetic theory. It does not address the congruence (X - 1)^n ≡ X^n - 1 or the condition n^2 ≡ 1 (mod r).

events.what_happened: Haining Fan (Tsinghua University and Zhongguancun Laboratory), 'An Improved Randomized AKS-class Primality Proving Algorithm', IACR ePrint 2026/051. It claims an improved sufficient condition for a randomised AKS-class algorithm, using congruences (x - s)^(n^j) ≡ x^(n^j) - s (mod x^e - r), with d the multiplicative order of n mod e. It claims time and space savings by factors between d^2 and d^3. The abstract does not mention Agrawal's conjecture. The ePrint record says the paper was withdrawn on 24 September 2026.
events.revisions: Received 2026-01-13. Withdrawn 2026-09-24 (per the ePrint record). The revision date is not listed on the page I read.
events.delivers: If valid, a faster sufficient condition for a randomised AKS-class test. It does not concern Agrawal's congruence.
events.doubts: Withdrawn, and I did not see the reason. I read the abstract only; the PDF returned HTTP 403.

disputes.summary: Origin of the conjecture. Wikipedia credits Rajat Bhattacharjee and Prashant Pandey, in their 2001 thesis. Grokipedia says an April 2001 B.Tech report 'Primality Testing' at IIT Kanpur, supervised by Agrawal. The Wikipedia 'List of conjectures' entry credits Manindra Agrawal. Agrawal's own talk slides list 'February 1999: A Conjecture', and a Fields Institute page refers to a 1999 conjecture of Agrawal and Biswas, which the AKS proof established. That 1999 conjecture is the AKS congruence, not this one. I have not resolved the attribution.

Hypotheses on r. Wikipedia and the 2003 AIM note take n and r to be coprime positive integers. Grokipedia gives the Popovych-style version with r prime and not dividing n, and says some presentations allow any coprime r. The Wikipedia AKS article says 'in some presentations' the same. The truth-value of the claim may depend on this choice, so it is recorded here.

Verification range. Wikipedia reports r < 100 and n < 10^10 (Kayal and Saxena, 2002) and r = 5 and n < 10^11 (Saxena, December 2014). Grokipedia gives n ≤ 10^11 for r < 100. I could not open the primary source for either claim.
Popovych's 2009 note. Wikipedia dates it 2008. The ePrint record says it was received on 5 January 2009 (ePrint 2009/008).

summary: Nothing since 26 January 2024 bears on this congruence. The searches found no proof, disproof, counterexample, or verification of the conjecture dated in the window, and no AI-related claim about it. The substantive record is older. (i) The March 2003 AIM note gives Lenstra's proposition: for explicitly constrained products of primes, n is a composite counterexample with r = 5, and the authors call the conjecture strongly suspected false. The note's abundance claim is a Lenstra–Pomerance heuristic, and no member of the family is exhibited. (ii) Popovych's 2009 ePrint extends that proposition to a more general case and states a different modified conjecture; the 2013 Carpathian paper gives subgroup lower bounds connected with it. (iii) Primaboinca searched 10^10 < n < 10^17 from 2010 until 31 May 2020 and found no counterexample. (iv) Wikipedia reports finite checks for r < 100 and n < 10^10, and for r = 5 and n < 10^11. I could not verify either from a primary source. The 2019 OEIS comment records that the Carmichael and Lucas-Carmichael route to a counterexample has no known term. The two in-window items touching AKS do not concern this congruence: Jalali and Ježil (arXiv April 2025) on AKS correctness in bounded arithmetic, and Fan (ePrint 2026/051, received January 2026, withdrawn 24 September 2026) on a randomised AKS-class condition. Close call: the Lenstra proposition is a genuine conditional construction, so the conjecture is strongly suspected false but not disproved. Whether it counts as settled-false depends on whether primes meeting the stated conditions exist, which is heuristic. Status is 'open, no proof or disproof'. Wikipedia's list entry for the problem is in the prime-numbers list and has no status note. The article's own status claim, seen via a search snippet, calls it an open problem. Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, says it remains unproven and was used only as a pointer. Attribution is disputed (see disputes). I did not establish the year posed, which is another pass's job. On AI: I found no system named in any source for this conjecture. My AI searches covered the problem's name with AI and LLM terms, lab announcements (OpenAI, Google DeepMind), 2026 AI-conjecture reports, Tao's Erdős-problem AI wiki (snippet only), breakthrough trackers, and arXiv 2026 AI papers. The AI results I found concern other problems: the May 2026 Erdős unit-distance disproof, Sra's 'GPT, the Counterexample Machine' (August 2026, which credits GPT Pro with counterexamples across several fields), and Axiom's February 2026 prime-regularity result. None mentions this congruence. Sra's paper was read only in part, and the human audit of OpenAI's proofs (arXiv 2608.14673) was read from its abstract.
competing_reading: Read the Lenstra proposition and the Lenstra–Pomerance heuristic as a substantive refutation in principle. The note gives an explicit conditional family of counterexamples for r = 5, the authors say the conjecture is strongly suspected false, the heuristic says counterexamples are abundant, and a 2019 OEIS comment records the same route. On this reading the problem is effectively settled as false, and a later pass may count the note as a resolution-type event. Against it: no member of the family has been exhibited, so no composite n with the congruence and n^2 ≢ 1 (mod r) is known. The question asks about all n, and the note offers only a heuristic for existence.
what_would_settle_it: An explicit composite n and coprime r with (X - 1)^n ≡ X^n - 1 (mod n, X^r - 1) and n^2 ≢ 1 (mod r). This is checkable in finite time by computing the congruence. Alternatively, a proof that primes meeting the Lenstra conditions exist for some k ≡ 1 (mod 4). Also needed: the full texts of Popovych 2009, to see what the 'more general case' covers; Váňa 2009, to see whether any counterexample or verification result is reported; the Kayal–Saxena 2002 report and the 2014 Saxena talk, to confirm the verification ranges; and a primary source for the Primaboinca r range.
